entries.title: Acronyms (Chapter Glossary)
do_not_test: Acronym list itself - reference material only, not an independently testable competency.
entries.zero_question_reason: Pure glossary/reference content, no clinical competency to assess.

entries.title: General Principles: Drug Nomenclature and Phases of Clinical Drug Testing

testable_competencies.nomenclature: Distinguish chemical, non-proprietary (generic), and proprietary (trade) drug names as background vocabulary used throughout the chapter and in prescribing communication.
testable_competencies.trial_phases: Recognize the pre-clinical through phase IV structure of drug development as background for interpreting cited RCT/trial evidence (supports SU-CP-19's landmark-trial context).

do_not_test: Exact DIN/NDC/DIN-HM/NPN regulatory-identifier distinctions - administrative detail beyond expected graduating-MD depth.

entries.title: Drug Administration: Routes and Selection

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Objective's enabling text explicitly requires the candidate to apply clinical pharmacology principles when prescribing, including 'prescribing appropriate routes, strengths, and quantities of medication' to mitigate adverse effects - a direct match to this unit's route-selection-by-patient-context content (e.g., parenteral route when NPO/vomiting/unconscious; sublingual/rectal to reduce first-pass exposure).

testable_competencies.route_selection: Select an appropriate route of drug administration given patient status (NPO, vomiting, unconscious, requires rapid onset, requires avoidance of first-pass metabolism) and recognize each route's principal risks (e.g., infection/extravasation for IV, erratic absorption for IM/SC, CSF leak for intrathecal).

entries.title: Pharmacokinetics Overview and Drug Absorption

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Objective requires applying clinical pharmacology principles to prescribing, including how comorbidities and organ function affect drug risk/benefit; bioavailability and first-pass effect are the mechanistic basis for common prescribing decisions (e.g., dose adjustment when switching a drug between IV and oral routes), though the objective does not name absorption pharmacokinetics explicitly.

testable_competencies.absorption_factors: Identify factors that alter drug absorption and bioavailability (lipophilicity, surface area, molecular size, ionization/pH, drug transporters) and their clinical consequences.
testable_competencies.first_pass: Apply the concept of first-pass metabolism to explain why oral bioavailability differs from IV bioavailability (F=1) and why some routes (sublingual, rectal, transdermal) are chosen specifically to reduce first-pass exposure.
testable_competencies.p_gp: Recognize P-glycoprotein as a clinically relevant efflux transporter whose inhibition (macrolides) or induction (rifampin, St. John's wort) alters serum concentrations of its substrates (digoxin, apixaban, cyclosporine).

entries.title: Drug Distribution (Volume of Distribution, Protein Binding, Depots, Barriers)

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Objective requires accounting for patient characteristics (age, organ function) when prescribing; Vd changes with age/body composition and altered protein binding in liver/kidney disease are the mechanistic basis for age- and disease-adjusted dosing, though not named explicitly in the objective text.

testable_competencies.vd_interpretation: Interpret a drug's volume of distribution as reflecting its tissue vs. plasma distribution pattern (small Vd -> plasma/protein-bound; large Vd -> tissue/fat depot), and apply this to explain age-related Vd changes for lipophilic drugs.
testable_competencies.barriers: Recognize the BBB and placenta as relative barriers relevant to CNS side-effect risk and fetal drug exposure.

entries.title: Drug Metabolism and Cytochrome P450-Mediated Interactions

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Objective's enabling text explicitly requires the candidate to 'apply principles of clinical pharmacology in prescribing medication' accounting for 'comorbidities, current medications, liver and renal function, genetics, age' and to 'recognize potential medical interactions when prescribing new medications' - a direct match to this unit's CYP-genotype (CYP2D6/CYP2C9) and CYP-inhibitor/inducer interaction content (erythromycin+simvastatin, grapefruit juice+CYP3A4 substrates, carbamazepine, rifampin/St. John's wort induction).

testable_competencies.biotransformation: Classify a drug-metabolism pathway as phase I (oxidation/reduction/hydrolysis, often CYP-mediated) or phase II (conjugation) and predict the consequence (activation of a prodrug, formation of a toxic metabolite, inactivation).
testable_competencies.cyp_interactions: Predict the clinical consequence of co-administering a CYP inhibitor or inducer with a CYP substrate drug (e.g., toxicity from inhibition, therapeutic failure from induction) using the named high-yield examples (macrolides, azole antifungals, grapefruit juice, rifampin, carbamazepine, St. John's wort).
testable_competencies.polymorphism: Recognize genetic CYP polymorphism (poor/ultra-rapid metabolizer) as a cause of unpredictable drug response, using the codeine/tramadol/tamoxifen (CYP2D6) and warfarin (CYP2C9) examples.

entries.title: Drug Excretion and Renal Elimination

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Objective requires accounting for 'liver and renal function' when prescribing; this unit's renal-clearance-mechanism content (glomerular filtration, tubular secretion/reabsorption, transporter-competition interactions such as probenecid-penicillin) is the mechanistic basis for renal dose adjustment.

testable_competencies.renal_clearance: Apply the renal clearance formula (filtration + secretion - reabsorption) to explain why renal impairment reduces clearance of renally-eliminated drugs, and recognize transporter-mediated excretion interactions (e.g., probenecid delaying penicillin excretion).

entries.title: Pharmacokinetic Parameters and Dosing Strategy (Half-Life, Clearance, Steady-State, Loading/Maintenance Dosing)

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Dosing-strategy selection (loading dose for urgency/long half-life, maintenance dosing, time to steady state) is the direct clinical operationalization of 'apply[ing] principles of clinical pharmacology in prescribing medication', and is explicitly enumerated content of this objective even though half-life/clearance formulas are not named verbatim.

testable_competencies.half_life: Apply the concept of elimination half-life to predict time to steady state (4-5 half-lives) and time to complete elimination after stopping a drug.
testable_competencies.loading_dose: Recognize when a loading dose is indicated (long half-life and/or need for rapid therapeutic effect, e.g., amiodarone, digoxin, phenytoin) vs. when maintenance dosing alone suffices.
testable_competencies.kinetics_order: Distinguish first-order from zero-order (non-linear/saturation) elimination kinetics and recognize the clinical drugs where zero-order kinetics becomes relevant at therapeutic or toxic doses (phenytoin, alcohol, high-dose ASA).

entries.title: Pharmacodynamics: Dose-Response, Efficacy, Potency, and Therapeutic Index

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Objective's enabling text requires 'assessment of the toxic effects on the patient' and understanding dose-toxicity relationships; the Therapeutic Index (TD50/ED50) and LD50/TD50 concepts tested in this unit are the quantitative framework underlying that toxicologic risk assessment, though the objective is framed around acute poisoning management rather than TI calculation itself.

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Objective requires the candidate to 'anticipate the potential for adverse effects and take steps to mitigate them' when prescribing; selecting a wide-TI drug preferentially over a narrow-TI one, where clinically equivalent, is a direct application of this enabling objective.

testable_competencies.efficacy_potency: Distinguish efficacy (Emax, maximal achievable response) from potency (EC50/ED50, the dose/concentration needed for a given response) and correctly interpret which of two drugs is more potent vs. more efficacious from a dose-response curve.
testable_competencies.therapeutic_index: Calculate/interpret the Therapeutic Index (TD50/ED50 or LD50/ED50) and apply the principle that a larger TI indicates a safer drug; recognize the named narrow-TI drugs that commonly require TDM (digoxin, theophylline, warfarin, lithium, cyclosporine).

do_not_test: Manual derivation of the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation or reading exact numeric EC50 values off a log(dose)-response graph - the testable concept is comparative interpretation (which drug is more potent/safer), not graph arithmetic.

entries.title: Drug-Receptor Interactions: Agonists and Antagonists

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Understanding whether a drug acts as an agonist, partial agonist, or antagonist (and by which mechanism) is foundational to 'apply[ing] principles of clinical pharmacology in prescribing medication', informing predictable clinical effects and reversal strategies, though the objective does not name receptor pharmacology explicitly.

testable_competencies.agonist_antagonist: Classify a drug as a full agonist, partial agonist, or antagonist (chemical, physiological, or pharmacological), and distinguish competitive-reversible from competitive-irreversible and non-competitive antagonism by their effect on a dose-response curve (rightward shift and overcomeable vs. reduced Emax and not overcomeable).
testable_competencies.clinical_examples: Apply the agonist/antagonist framework to named clinical examples (naloxone as a reversible competitive antagonist at opioid receptors; buprenorphine as a partial mu-opioid agonist).

entries.title: Variability in Drug Response

testable_competencies.variability_sources: Recognize the categories of interindividual drug-response variability (intake/adherence, absorption, PK/PD drug interactions, distribution, biotransformation/elimination, PD sensitivity) as the rationale for why some patients require individualized dosing or therapeutic drug monitoring (supports SU-CP-12).

entries.title: Therapeutic Drug Monitoring

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Objective's enabling text requires the candidate to 'apply principles of clinical pharmacology in prescribing medication' and to 'review... adherence and effectiveness of the patient's current medications' - TDM is the concrete mechanism for individualizing and verifying medication effectiveness for the named narrow-TI drugs, a direct match to this unit's content.

testable_competencies.tdm_indications: Recognize which clinical scenarios warrant therapeutic drug monitoring (low therapeutic index, unpredictable dose-response, high consequence of toxicity/failure, wide interpatient PK variability) and identify the drugs that commonly require it (digoxin, phenytoin, vancomycin, aminoglycosides, lithium, warfarin).
testable_competencies.sampling_timing: Recognize that TDM sampling is most informative once steady-state has been reached (~4-5 half-lives).

entries.title: Adverse Drug Reactions: Classification and Clinical Approach

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Objective's enabling text explicitly requires the candidate to 'anticipate the potential for adverse effects and take steps to mitigate them' and to 'provide them [patients] with information about any adverse effects, how to report them, and what they should do if adverse effects occur' - a direct match to this unit's Type A-E ADR classification and history/reporting-workflow content.

mcc_evidence.objective_title: Leader/Manager - Demonstrate leadership on health care teams and contribute to high-quality patient care by enhancing patient safety
mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (role-level record; no per-objective ID exists for this role)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Group's enabling text requires contributing to patient safety through health-system participation; the Canadian Adverse Drug Reaction Monitoring Program / MedEffect Canada reporting pathway described in this unit is the concrete system-level mechanism for that safety contribution.

testable_competencies.adr_classification: Classify a suspected adverse drug reaction using the Type A-E framework (Augmented/dose-related, Bizarre/idiosyncratic, Chronic/cumulative, Delayed, End-of-use/withdrawal) to predict its likely mechanism and management approach.
testable_competencies.approach: Take a structured history (timing, de-challenge/re-challenge, complete medication history including OTC/natural health products) to evaluate a suspected ADR and distinguish drug effect from underlying disease.
testable_competencies.reporting: Recognize which suspected ADRs require formal reporting (unexpected, serious, or reactions to drugs on the market <5 years) and the Canadian reporting pathway (MedEffect Canada / Canada Vigilance).

clinical_source_organizations: Health Canada (MedEffect Canada / Canada Vigilance Adverse Reaction Monitoring Program)

entries.title: Drug Interactions (Mechanisms and Clinically Significant Examples)

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Objective's enabling text explicitly instructs the candidate to 'recognize potential medical interactions when prescribing new medications' - a direct, verbatim match to this unit's core content.

testable_competencies.pk_vs_pd: Classify a drug interaction mechanism as pharmacokinetic (altered absorption/distribution/metabolism/excretion) or pharmacodynamic (additive/synergistic or antagonistic effects).
testable_competencies.named_interactions: Recognize the clinical consequence of the chapter's named high-yield interaction pairs (warfarin + macrolide/quinolone/TMP-SMX/metronidazole -> increased INR; warfarin + acetaminophen -> increased INR with chronic high-dose use; OCP + rifampin -> contraceptive failure; sildenafil + nitrates -> severe hypotension; SSRI + St. John's wort/MAOI -> serotonin syndrome; statin + macrolide/azole/fibrate/niacin -> rhabdomyolysis; TMP-SMX + ACEi/ARB/spironolactone -> hyperkalemia).

entries.title: Autonomic Nervous System Physiology and Pharmacology

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Understanding which autonomic receptor subtype mediates a given organ effect is foundational to 'apply[ing] principles of clinical pharmacology in prescribing medication' for any sympathomimetic, sympatholytic, parasympathomimetic, or anticholinergic drug class, though the objective does not name autonomic receptor pharmacology explicitly.

testable_competencies.receptor_mapping: Match an autonomic receptor subtype (beta1, beta2, alpha1, alpha2, M1, M2, M3) to its organ location and physiologic effect (e.g., beta1 -> increased cardiac contractility/HR; beta2 -> bronchodilation; M3 -> sweat gland stimulation) to predict the effect of a drug acting at that receptor.
testable_competencies.termination: Recognize the mechanisms terminating ACh (acetylcholinesterase/pseudocholinesterase) and NE (reuptake, MAO, COMT) action, and apply this to acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor use (myasthenia gravis, Alzheimer's disease).

entries.title: Opioid Therapy for Chronic Non-Cancer Pain

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Objective's enabling text requires the candidate to 'address polypharmacy and the options for deprescribing' and to consider dose/quantity/route when prescribing to mitigate adverse effects - a direct match to this unit's opioid-dose-ceiling and collaborative-tapering content.

mcc_evidence.objective_title: Leader/Manager - Abide by the regulatory requirements governing medical office practice (maintenance of patient records, guidelines concerning prescriptions, especially narcotics)
mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (role-level record; no per-objective ID exists for this role)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Group's enabling text names narcotic-prescribing regulatory compliance explicitly; the national Canadian opioid-therapy guideline cited in this unit is the concrete clinical-practice guideline that operationalizes that regulatory obligation for chronic non-cancer pain.

testable_competencies.initiation: Apply the principle of optimizing non-opioid pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic therapy before initiating opioid therapy for chronic non-cancer pain.
testable_competencies.dose_limits: Apply Canadian guideline dose thresholds (<90 MME/day, ideally <50 MME/day at initiation) and recognize when a slow, collaborative taper is indicated (>=90 MME/day).

clinical_source_organizations: Canadian guideline for opioid therapy and chronic non-cancer pain (Busse et al., CMAJ 2017)

entries.title: Common Drug Endings (Suffix-to-Class Recognition)

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Recognizing a drug's class from its name supports safe prescribing (avoiding within-class duplication, anticipating class-level interactions/adverse effects) as implied by the objective's broader prescribing-safety scope, though drug-suffix nomenclature is not named explicitly.

testable_competencies.suffix_recognition: Infer a drug's pharmacologic class from its name ending (e.g., -olol, -pril, -sartan, -statin, -azole, -caine, -mab) to anticipate its mechanism, indications, and class-typical adverse effects/interactions, while recognizing the chapter's documented exceptions (methimazole, itraconazole, nystatin).

entries.title: Dangerous Abbreviations, Symbols, and Dose Designations

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Objective's enabling text explicitly requires the candidate to 'discuss error mitigation strategies' as part of a patient-safety-focused approach to care; the ISMP Canada dangerous-abbreviation list and its recommended corrections (e.g., 'use unit' not 'U', always use a leading zero) is precisely such a concrete, chapter-specific error-mitigation strategy.

mcc_evidence.official_source: research/mcc/objectives_registry.json (retrieved from official MCC Objectives Online Web Service)
mcc_evidence.mapping_rationale: Objective's enabling text requires 'generating a clear and legible prescription that meets legal requirements' and 'recognizing common cases of medication errors and how they can be prevented' - directly matching this unit's content.

testable_competencies.error_prone_terms: Recognize the ISMP Canada list of dangerous abbreviations, symbols, and dose designations (U, IU, QD/QOD, trailing zeros, lack of leading zero, ambiguous drug abbreviations) and apply the recommended safe alternative when writing or reviewing a prescription/order.

clinical_source_organizations: Institute for Safe Medication Practices Canada (ISMP Canada)

entries.title: Landmark Pharmacology Trials
do_not_test: Named-trial results/statistics (CoumaGen-II, rivaroxaban QT study) - historical trial trivia, not an independent clinical competency.
entries.zero_question_reason: Historical trial citations/results tables, not a clinical competency - matches the explicit do-not-test treatment given to the equivalent landmark-trials sections in Chapters A and C.
